issues.legal_issue: A claimant without documentary title can recover immovable property on the basis of prior possession only by proving settled possession, and cannot prevail over a defendant who establishes a better title.
material_facts: The plaintiff had no title document and sought possession based on alleged prior possession and dispossession within twelve years before filing suit.
The evidence relied on by the plaintiff did not establish possession of the disputed plot: the rent note did not identify that plot, and only a small part of a vehicle body lay on its boundary.

The First Appellate Court found that the defendant’s predecessor had possessed the property before selling it to the defendant, and that the defendant had proved title and possession through the sale deeds and other evidence.
The Supreme Court found no material establishing the plaintiff’s settled or established possession and upheld the First Appellate Court’s findings.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiff failed to prove possessory title or a right to recover possession; the suit was dismissed and the First Appellate Court’s judgment was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Section 64 of the Limitation Act, 1963 permits a suit for possession based on previous possession, brought within twelve years of dispossession, without initially relying on proprietary title. Under Nair Service Society Ltd. v. K.C. Alexander, AIR 1968 SC 1165, where a defendant sets up title, the claimant must establish a better title; prior peaceful possession can itself support a claim where no better title is shown. Rame Gowda v. M. Varadappa Naidu, (2004) 1 SCC 769, explains that settled possession can be protected even against the rightful owner, but it must be effective, undisturbed, and known to the owner or not concealed, and must involve animus possidendi. Stray or casual acts of trespass do not establish settled possession. Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 (corresponding to Section 9 of the 1877 Act) concerns the distinct summary remedy for recovery based on possession without adjudicating title. The judgment also refers to Midnapur Zamindary Co. Ltd. v. Naresh Narayan Roy, AIR 1924 PC 144, for the principle that possession must be obtained through legal process rather than force.

predicates.possessory_recovery_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking recovery of immovable property on the basis of alleged prior possession.
predicates.claimant_failed_to_prove_settled_possess: The claimant’s evidence did not establish effective, undisturbed possession of the property for a sufficient period with the owner’s knowledge or without concealment.
predicates.defendant_established_better_title: The defendant established a better title to the property through evidence of title and possession, including the possession of a predecessor in title.

issues.definition: When a claimant seeks recovery based on prior possession but fails to prove settled possession and the defendant establishes a better title, the claimant is not entitled to recover possession.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court deciding a second appeal should not interfere with the First Appellate Court’s findings of fact when they are supported by the evidence and are neither perverse nor contrary to the record.
material_facts: The First Appellate Court found, on its assessment of the evidence, that the defendant had proved title and possession and that the plaintiff had not proved settled possession.
The High Court interfered with the First Appellate Court’s judgment, but the Supreme Court found no fault with that court’s factual findings and held that they were supported by the record.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in interfering with the First Appellate Court’s findings; its judgment was set aside and the First Appellate Court’s judgment was restored.
issues.legal_principle: The Court stated that a High Court should generally not interfere in a second appeal with findings of fact recorded by the First Appellate Court when those findings are based on the evidence and are not perverse or against the material on record.

predicates.second_appeal_from_first_appellate_judgm: The matter before the High Court was a second appeal challenging a judgment of the First Appellate Court.
predicates.first_appellate_findings_based_on_eviden: The First Appellate Court based its factual findings on the evidence in the record.
predicates.findings_not_perverse_or_contrary_to_rec: The First Appellate Court’s findings were neither perverse nor contrary to the material in the record.

issues.definition: In a second appeal, when the First Appellate Court based its findings on the evidence and those findings are not perverse or contrary to the record, the High Court should not interfere with them.
